items.title: CVE-2026-114119 — Best Practice Software Bp Premier before 1.14.1.1128 uses a hardcoded Microsoft SQL Server…
items.body:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-114119 (score CVSS 9.8).

Best Practice Software Bp Premier before 1.14.1.1128 uses a hardcoded Microsoft SQL Server administrative password that is shared across all installations and cannot be changed without breaking the application. Attackers with network access to the database instance can authenticate as sysadmin, bypass application authentication, and execute operating system commands as SYSTEM.

Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

The CDE released multiple statements over the last week warning the state’s students that assessment contractor Educational Testing Service (ETS) suffered a months-long data breach.

A cyberattack on a contractor for California’s Department of Education (CDE) exposed troves of sensitive information covering all children enrolled in public schools over the last three years.

The CDE released multiple statements over the last week warning the state’s students that assessment contractor Educational Testing Service (ETS) suffered a months-long data breach.

Those affected include current and former students enrolled in California public schools between 2023 and the current school year, as well as students who left a California school since 2006 and did not confirm transfer to another school with the CDE.

CDE hired ETS to provide testing to California K-12 public schools, which enrolled more than 5.7 million students in the 2025 school year. ETS manages the California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) and the English Language Proficiency Assessments for California (ELPAC) exams given each year.

ETS, which did not respond to requests for comment, said in a release that hackers copied student information through a secure file transfer protocol site this year from May 22 to September 18.

After discovering the breach on September 25, ETS initially disabled the account used to steal the information and eventually took the entire site offline before building an entirely new platform in response to the hack.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a settlement under which 23andMe's successor will pay $6 million to resolve allegations that the company did not properly protect customers' data before a 2023 breach.

The settlement is pending approval by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in the Eastern District of Missouri and ensures affected consumers maintain the right to delete their data and order genetic samples be destroyed, according to a press release Monday from California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

In March 2025, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy and sold customers’ saliva samples and genetic data to the TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit created by 23andMe’s former founder and CEO Anne Wojkicki.

In addition to running 23andMe, Wojcicki is the CEO of the Chrome Holding Company, the entity that settled with Bonta.

A spokesperson for TTAM said in a statement that the organization is a “newly established independent nonprofit organization and is not involved in matters related to Chrome Holding Co., formerly known as 23andMe, Inc.”

“The institute was not involved in the matters and has no role in the settlement.”

Chrome Holding Company does not have any personnel authorized to speak to the media, according to a staffer answering the phone.

The UK public sector has reached a cyber resilience inflection point. A Nigerian national who worked with a group to hack tax prep businesses and conduct millions of dollars in fraud using customer data was sentenced this week.

A hacker who took part in attacks on tax preparation businesses was sentenced to eight years in federal prison and ordered to pay back millions of dollars in damages after pleading guilty to multiple charges.

Nigerian national Chukwuemeka Amachukwu was extradited from France last year on fraud, hacking and identity theft charges.

Prosecutors accused Amachukwu of leading a group that used spearphishing emails to breach tax preparation businesses dating back to 2019.

“Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into U.S. businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “These crimes imposed significant harm on the victims and the public, and so it is only appropriate that the crimes also come with a significant sentence for the defendant.”

Court documents showed Amachukwu worked with Kingsley Uchelue Utulu and other Nigeria-based hackers to break into the tax businesses and steal information on about 800 business customers.

One incident took place in May 2021, when the men sent a phishing email to an employee of a Manhattan-based tax preparation business, infecting the company with malware. Once inside, the men allegedly stole the tax information of the business’ customers and used it to take a number of fraudulent actions.

Signal de veille — The Register.

Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans, officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP
